result.summary: Ajax and Ulysses plead before the Greek chiefs for the armour of Achilles. Ulysses wins, and Ajax kills himself, his blood turning into a purple flower. Ulysses then fetches Philoctetes and the arrows of Hercules, Troy falls, Hecuba is carried off, and Polymnestor murders Polydorus.

scenes.title: Argument of the Book
scenes.summary: A prose summary of the events of the section.

scenes.title: Ajax Pleads for the Arms
scenes.summary: Ajax claims the arms of Achilles by birth and by deeds, and attacks Ulysses as a coward, a deceiver and the destroyer of Palamedes.
scenes.stakes: Ajax risks losing the arms and his honour to a rival he despises.

scenes.title: Ulysses Answers
scenes.summary: Ulysses answers with his own birth, his cunning in finding Achilles, his embassies and his night raids. He promises to bring Philoctetes and shows the stolen statue of Minerva.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses stands to lose the prize and his reputation if the chiefs prefer brute strength to wisdom.

scenes.title: Death of Ajax
scenes.summary: The chiefs award the arms to Ulysses. Ajax kills himself with his sword and a purple flower springs from his blood. Ulysses fetches Philoctetes and the arrows from Lemnos.
scenes.stakes: Ajax loses his honour, and with it his life.

scenes.title: The Fall of Troy
scenes.summary: Troy burns, Priam is killed and the Trojan women are carried off. Hecuba takes Hector's ashes and leaves her hair on his tomb.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans lose their city, their families and their freedom.

scenes.title: Polymnestor Murders Polydorus
scenes.summary: Polydorus, sent to Thrace with treasure, is killed by Polymnestor for his gold once Troy is ruined.
scenes.stakes: Polydorus loses his life to a greedy host.

alias_notes.explanation: Alternate name for the king of the gods.
Epithet from Mount Cyllene, his birthplace.
Refers to Ulysses' island realm of Dulichium.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses sums up his case: mind outranks body, as helmsman outranks rower.
Famous judgment: eloquence prevails and the fluent man gets the arms of the brave.
Poignant farewell of the Trojan women leaving their burning city.

analysis.text: The contest sets brute strength against cunning and eloquence. Ovid lets rhetoric win, and the result is Ajax's tragedy.
The speeches follow the Roman rhetorical exercise of the suasoria and controversia, in which paired opposing speeches were composed.

legacy.text: Ajax and Ulysses' debate echoes Sophocles' Ajax and later inspired Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida and many rhetoric exercises.
The hyacinth marked with the letters AI, linking Ajax's name to lament, became a standard poetic image.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's version of the speeches is far longer than the brief debate in Homer's Odyssey, where Ajax's ghost refuses to speak to Ulysses.

language_notes.text: Ajax's shield was said to be made of seven layers of ox-hide, which is why he is called lord of the seven-fold shield.
Sigæan shores: Sigeum, the headland near Troy where the Greek ships were drawn up.
Pelasgians: an old name for the Greeks, used here as a general term for the Greek army.
Telamon joined Hercules in taking Troy, and sailed on the ship Argo (the Pagasæan ship) to Colchis. Æacus became a judge of the dead.
Ulysses feigned madness by ploughing the sand to avoid joining the war. Palamedes exposed the trick by placing Ulysses' infant son in front of the plough.
Philoctetes, son of Pœas, was abandoned on Lemnos after a snakebite left him with a foul wound. Ajax says Ulysses deserves the same suffering.
Ulysses took revenge on Palamedes by burying gold in his tent and forging a letter, so that Palamedes appeared to be a traitor and was stoned.
Ajax lists Ulysses' night raids, such as the capture of Rhesus' horses and the killing of the spy Dolon, to belittle them.
Dulichian: from Dulichium, an island near Ithaca belonging to Ulysses' realm.
Caitiff: an archaic word for a wretched coward.
The Laërtian hero is Ulysses, son of Laërtes. Ajax, the son of Telamon, has just finished his own speech claiming Achilles' arms.
Pelasgians: here a poetic name for the Greeks generally, not the ancient Pelasgian people.
Ajax claims descent from Jove through Aeacus and Telamon; Ulysses matches this with his own line from Jove through Arcesius and Laërtes.
Condemned and banished: Telamon and Peleus were exiled for killing their half-brother Phocus. Ulysses taunts Ajax with this family crime.
Cyllenian Mercury: Mercury was born on Mount Cyllene. In this tradition he is the father of Ulysses' mother, Anticlea.
Pyrrhus is Achilles' son, also called Neoptolemus. As Achilles' direct heir he outranks Ajax's claim by kinship.
Thetis knew Achilles would die at Troy, so she hid him disguised as a girl at Scyros among the king's daughters.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, often used for the whole city.
At Aulis the fleet was becalmed because Diana was angry. Agamemnon was told to sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia to her.
Ulysses sarcastically addresses Ajax as 'thou' ('wast', 'knowest'), the archaic singular form, mocking him as a mere fighter.
Refers to Jove's deceptive dream sent to Agamemnon, who then tested the army by ordering a retreat, as told in the Iliad.
Thersites was the ugly, abusive common soldier of the Iliad whom Ulysses beat with the sceptre for insulting the kings.
Diomedes, son of Tydeus, was Ulysses' partner in the night raid on the Trojan camp.
Dolon was a Trojan spy captured by Ulysses and Diomedes, who gave up Trojan plans before being killed.
Rhesus was a Thracian king whose famous horses were stolen by Ulysses and Diomedes, because an oracle said Troy could not fall if they drank from the Xanthus.
The 'descendant of Actor' is Patroclus, who wore Achilles' armour to drive the Trojans from the ships and was killed by Hector.
Ajax was one of nine champions who drew lots to fight Hector, as in the Iliad.
The shield's engravings (sea, earth, stars, cities) are the scenes Vulcan made on Achilles' new armour; Ajax is said to be too dull to grasp them.
"The Bear that avoids the sea": the constellation never sets below the horizon into the ocean, according to ancient belief.
Ulysses found Achilles hidden among women at Scyros, where Thetis had disguised him to keep him from the war.
Palamedes exposed Ulysses' feigned madness; Ulysses later framed him with forged Trojan gold and letters, and he was stoned as a traitor.
Philoctetes was left on Lemnos because of his festering snake-bite wound; Ulysses was blamed for the abandonment.
The Dardanian prophet is Helenus, a Trojan seer Ulysses captured, who revealed that Troy needed Philoctetes' arrows (Hercules' bow) and the Palladium.
The statue is the Palladium, an image of Minerva (Greek Pallas Athena) whose presence was believed to protect Troy.
The son of Tydeus is Diomedes, who accompanied Ulysses on the night raid to steal the Palladium.
The brother of the greater son of Atreus is Menelaus; the "greater" son is Agamemnon. Both lists name Greek heroes who might have claimed the arms.
The Œbalian wound is that of Hyacinthus, a youth of Œbalia (Sparta), killed by Apollo's discus; the hyacinth flower sprang from his blood.
The petals bear the letters AI, which are Ajax's initial letters and also the Greek cry of grief, 'ai, ai'.
Hypsipyle and Thoas ruled Lemnos; its women had killed their husbands, hence the 'infamous' slaughter. The Tirynthian hero is Hercules, whose arrows Philoctetes held.
Hecuba, Priam's wife, was turned into a dog, which explains her 'barkings' in a foreign land.
The priestess of Apollo is Cassandra, dragged from Minerva's altar by Ajax the Lesser.
Boreas is the north wind.
Dulichian means from Dulichium, an island in Ulysses' realm; here it refers to Ulysses' men.
Bistonia is Thrace; the Bistones were a Thracian people.

context_notes.text: Achilles' divine armour, made by Vulcan, is awarded to the best of the Greeks. The Greek chiefs judge between Ajax and Ulysses.
Ajax counts the line as Jupiter, Æacus, Telamon, Ajax. Achilles, son of Peleus, is at the same distance from Jupiter.
Nestor was the oldest Greek leader, famed for wise and persuasive speech. Ulysses once left him behind when his horse was wounded.
Hector was the greatest Trojan warrior. Ajax fought him in a duel and also drove him back from the Greek ships.
Ulysses says he brought Achilles to the Greek army, though Achilles was fated to die at Troy.
Agamemnon, son of Atreus, is present as judge. Ulysses flatters him while taking credit for persuading him to give up Iphigenia.
Antenor was a Trojan elder who favored returning Helen. Ulysses and Menelaüs went to Troy to demand her before the war.
The 'son of Atreus' is Agamemnon, commander of the Greek army; the 'son of Telamon' is Ajax, Ulysses' rival for the arms.
Showing scars to a crowd was a traditional way for a Roman speaker to prove his service.
Ulysses claims credit for rescuing Achilles' body, a deed Ajax also claims, since both defended the corpse.
The "azure mother" is Thetis, a sea nymph and mother of Achilles, who had Vulcan forge the arms now being contested.
The Simoïs is a river near Troy and Ida its mountain; Ulysses lists impossibilities to show how absurd it would be to rely on Ajax.
Ajax's famous shield was made of seven layers of bull hide, as described in the Iliad.
Ajax lost the contest for Achilles' arms to Ulysses and, driven mad by rage and shame, turns to suicide.
Astyanax was Hector's infant son; the Greeks threw him from the walls so he could not avenge Troy.
Polydorus was Priam's youngest son, sent to Thrace with gold for safety during the war.

literary_notes.text: Ajax is introduced by his seven-fold shield, an epithet that stresses his strength as a warrior and prepares for his bluntness.
Ajax sets his own talent for fighting against Ulysses' talent for talking. This shapes the whole speech as a contest between deeds and words.
The question presents Ajax's grievance as obvious injustice, and he mocks Ulysses' cowardice by recalling the feigned madness.
Ajax suddenly addresses the absent Philoctetes, which gives his anger a dramatic and emotional turn.
Ajax sarcastically says that Ulysses fights by getting rid of his own comrades, and so turns Ulysses' reputation for cunning into a charge of treachery.
The word 'forsooth' mocks Ulysses, and the line sets Ajax's real defence of a thousand ships against Ulysses' talk.
Ajax claims the great shield with the whole world on it cannot suit Ulysses' left hand, which he calls formed for theft.
The narrator presents Ulysses as a studied orator, pausing and lowering his eyes. This sets up the calculated persuasion of his speech.
The parenthetical shows Ulysses wiping his eyes as if weeping. The narrator hints that his grief is performed to win the judges.
Ulysses pretends to ask only for fairness and to disown his own cleverness, while he stresses Ajax's stupidity and his own eloquence.
Mixing arms among women's trinkets was a trap. Ulysses presents his cunning as a test that reveals Achilles' real nature.
The repeated 'twas I' (anaphora) piles up claims, so that Achilles' victories become Ulysses' own.
Ulysses attacks Ajax with a barrage of questions, implying he did nothing useful.
Ulysses sarcastically praises Ajax's 'grand' words, suggesting that Ajax is all boast and no action.
Ulysses presents himself as the eloquent leader who can turn grief into persuasion and save the army.
Ulysses mocks the idea of denying him the arms, while turning the stolen horses of Rhesus into proof of his worth.
The repeated 'on these shoulders' stresses his physical effort, and suggests that he is no mere talker.
Ulysses opens with sarcasm, mocking the idea that a crude soldier could value or understand the divine artistry of the armour.
The balanced "both of us dissembled" turns Ajax's charge back on him and on Achilles, using tight parallel phrasing.
Impossible events, such as rivers flowing backward, stress the certainty that Ajax's stupidity could never serve the Greeks as Ulysses can.
Ulysses suddenly addresses the absent Philoctetes, dramatising his determination and showing his persuasive rhetoric.
The helmsman and rower, and general and soldier, illustrate the superiority of mind over body in Ulysses' self-presentation.
The speech ends with the sudden reveal of the Palladium as physical proof, giving the oration a theatrical climax.
The warrior who resisted every enemy is overcome by his own grief; the repeated 'alone' stresses his isolation.
The flower recalls Hyacinthus, linking two deaths through the same metamorphosis and making Ajax's end a lament.
Hecuba is shown as a 'dreadful sight' among tombs, defined by grief and loss.
The praise of a wise plan, qualified by the added gold, signals the betrayal to come.
